name: In the Heat of the Night
s: Based on the critically acclaimed novel of the same name, this series provided a hopeful, yet honest look at life in the new South. Set in the fictional Sparta, Mississippi, the show was a marvelous blend of heartfelt drama and folksy humor. It portrayed both the professional and personal pursuits of Sparta P.D's officers.

paragraphs.text: In the Heat of the Night is an American police procedural crime drama television broadcast 1988 to 1995, starring Carroll O'Connor and Howard Rollins.

It was loosely based on the Academy Award -winning 1967 film of the same title directed by Norman Jewison, starring Sidney Poitier and Rod Steiger and was in turn inspired by the 1965 novel by John Ball.

The TV series starred O'Connor as Southern police chief William "Bill" Gillespie and Rollins as Philadelphia police detective Virgil Tibbs. The series was broadcast on NBC from March 6, 1988, to May 19, 1992, then it moved to CBS from October 28, 1992 to May 16, 1995. Its executive producers were O'Connor, Fred Silverman and Juanita Bartlett.
This series marked O'Connor's return to a series for the first time since the All in the Family spin-off Archie Bunker's Place ended in 1983.

Set in the late 1980s–1990s, the series acts as a sequel to the 1967 film but with a floating timeline. It carried over three core characters — Virgil Tibbs, Chief Gillespie, and Courtney (renamed Parker) — and relied on the movie's fame to set the foundation. The show gained acclaim for the chemistry between its leads, engaging crime plots, and relevant social commentary.

To develop it as a weekly series, there were obvious changes that would have to justify Virgil Tibbs returning to Sparta, a racially divided small town in Mississippi. In the film, Tibbs was a police detective from Philadelphia who became embroiled in a murder investigation while passing through town. For the series, he becomes a Sparta native who moved North after high school, became a police officer, got married, and returned to his hometown — which he now views as backwards and slow. In the film, Gillespie was unmarried. The series establishes him as a World War II veteran and widower who tragically lost his Italian war bride and infant son during childbirth decades earlier.

In the pilot episode, Philadelphia detective Virgil Tibbs returns home to Sparta, Mississippi, for his mother's funeral. Mayor James Findlay persuades him to stay on as Chief of Detectives — partly to modernize the racially divided, underskilled police force, and partly to bolster Findlay's own congressional campaign. The blustery older "good old boy", police Chief Bill Gillespie, who knows Tibbs from a prior murder case, resents the appointment, suspecting it is a political maneuver to replace him.
